title: SwiftUI and UIKit together
summary: Show SwiftUI inside UIKit with `UIHostingController`. Show UIKit inside SwiftUI with `UIViewRepresentable` / `UIViewControllerRepresentable` plus a `Coordinator` for delegates.
body: **In simple words:** Most real apps are mixed. New screens are often SwiftUI, old ones UIKit. Apple gives bridges in both directions.

**SwiftUI in UIKit:** `let vc = UIHostingController(rootView: ProfileView())` and push it like any view controller. Inside collection view cells, use `cell.contentConfiguration = UIHostingConfiguration { RowView() }`.

**UIKit in SwiftUI:** conform to `UIViewRepresentable`. `makeUIView` creates the view once. `updateUIView` copies SwiftUI state into the UIKit view (runs often, must be cheap). `makeCoordinator` creates an object that acts as the delegate and sends changes back through a `Binding`.

**Migration strategy:** new screens in SwiftUI, shared design-system components available in both, rewrite old screens only when you are already changing them a lot. Keep one owner of navigation (often UIKit coordinators hosting SwiftUI screens).
**Common issues:** hosting controller sizing (`sizingOptions = .intrinsicContentSize`), safe area doubled, keyboard avoidance, and SwiftUI environment values not crossing into UIKit automatically.
keyPoints: `UIViewRepresentable`: make, update (cheap and idempotent), coordinator for delegates.
Migrate screen by screen; keep navigation ownership in one place.
Keep UIKit where SwiftUI is still weak (complex lists, text editing, fine scroll control).

mistakes: Creating the UIKit view inside `updateUIView` (recreated every update).
Setting values in `updateUIView` unconditionally, causing loops or cursor jumps.
followups: **How do you decide when to rewrite a UIKit screen in SwiftUI?** When it needs big changes anyway, SwiftUI supports what it needs on your minimum iOS, and performance is measured to be fine.
